e-477.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
e-477.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-478.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a $\tan^2{x}$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
\tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\tan x -x+C.	
	}
$$

e-479.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\cot^2 x &=\csc^2 x -1.
}
$$

Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(5\cot^2 x -x^2\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \bigg(5\left(\csc^2 x -1 \right) -x^2\bigg) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\int \left(5\csc^2 x -5 -x^2\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=-5\cot x -5x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.	
	}
$$

e-480.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities
e-480.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta$ with $\theta = 3x,$ we get 

$$
\eqalign{
		1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
		\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                &= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                 &= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
				                                &= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
                                                                 &= 	\dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
	}
$$

decision.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by 1+sin(x): 1/(1−sin(x)) = (1+sin(x))/cos²(x) = sec²(x)+sec(x)tan(x). Integrating gives tan(x)+sec(x)+C.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡x=1-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡x=1-{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
content.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡x=1-{cos}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({csc}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.$ 
Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-1}=\frac{1}{-{sin}^{2}⁡x}=-{csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{5\pi }{6}-\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3} \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We are using the identity

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x+1={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.

$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Secant-Tangent Identity
content.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }({cos}^{3}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x{cos}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0-0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x({sec}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡x(1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x(1+\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x(1+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C\end{aligned}

decision.explanation: Using 1+tan²(x)=sec²(x), the integrand becomes 4sec²(x)−3x². Integrating gives 4tan(x)−x³+C, matching option e.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x+1={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3{x}^{2}+4{tan}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4-3{x}^{2}+4({sec}^{2}⁡x-1))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (4-3{x}^{2}+4{sec}^{2}⁡x-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (-3{x}^{2}+4{sec}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C \\  & =-{x}^{3}+4\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

decision.explanation: Using cot²(x)=csc²(x)−1, an antiderivative is −cot(x)−x. Evaluating from π/4 to π/2 gives −π/2−(−1−π/4)=1−π/4.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{cot}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}({csc}^{2}⁡x-1)\text{d}x \\  & =(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x-x){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =[-0-\frac{\pi }{2}]-[-1-\frac{\pi }{4}] \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+1+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Writing u=5x−2, the denominator is sin(u)(1+cot²(u))=sin(u)csc²(u)=1/sin(u). The integrand therefore becomes sin(5x−2), whose antiderivative is −cos(5x−2)/5+C.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ with $\theta =5x-2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)={csc}^{2}⁡(5x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{[{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)+1]\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{{csc}^{2}⁡(5x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(5x-2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)\text{d}x & = \\ -\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-2)+C & .\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =2x+\frac{\pi }{6},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ {tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$

content.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =2x+\frac{\pi }{6},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ {tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6}) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})\text{d}x & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})-1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})\text{d}x-\int 1\cdot \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{6})-x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})}{{sec}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi /3} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =0-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}

decision.explanation: Let u=2x+π/5. The denominator is cos(u)(tan²(u)+1)=cos(u)sec²(u)=1/cos(u), so the integrand is cos(2x+π/5). Its antiderivative is sin(2x+π/5)/2+C.

after.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ with $\theta =2x+\frac{\pi }{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{[{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+1]\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\text{d}x & = \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+C & .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Calculate ∫1tan2⁡(2x+π5)cos⁡(2x+π5)+cos⁡(2x+π5)dx.

a
−12tan⁡(2x+π5)+C
b
2sin⁡(2x+π5)+C
c
−12sin⁡(2x+π5)+C
d
2sec⁡(2x+π5)+C
e
12sin⁡(2x+π5)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

From the identity 1+tan2⁡θ=sec2⁡θ, with θ=2x+π5, we get 1+tan2⁡(2x+π5)=sec2⁡(2x+π5).

Substituting the above into our integral gives ∫1tan2⁡(2x+π5)cos⁡(2x+π5)+cos⁡(2x+π5)dx=∫1[tan2⁡(2x+π5)+1]cos⁡(2x+π5)dx=∫1sec2⁡(2x+π5)cos⁡(2x+π5)dx=∫cos2⁡(2x+π5)cos⁡(2x+π5)dx=∫cos⁡(2x+π5)dx=12sin⁡(2x+π5)+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Trigonometric Expressions With Linear Arguments Using the Pythagorean Identities
content.worked_solution:
From the identity $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ with $\theta =2x+\frac{\pi }{5},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})={sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{[{tan}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+1]\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{{sec}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{{cos}^{2}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})\text{d}x & = \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+\frac{\pi }{5})+C & .\end{aligned}
$$
